AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: This study investigated the effects of short-term glucocorticoid administration on voluntary activation and intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory circuits.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Seventeen healthy men participated in a pseudo randomized double-blind study to receive either dexamethasone (8 mg·d, n = 9 subjects) or placebo (n = 8 subjects) for 7 days. The ankle dorsiflexion torque, corresponding electromyography (EMG) of the tibialis anterior, and voluntary activation assessed by the interpolated twitch method using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) were measured during a maximal voluntary contraction (MVC). Short-latency intracortical inhibition (SICI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were assessed at rest and during submaximal contraction (50% MVC torque) by paired-pulse TMS with the conditioning stimulus set at 0.8x of motor threshold (0.8x MT) and delivered 2 ms (SICI) and 13 ms (ICF) prior to the test stimulus (1.2x MT).

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The MVC torque (+14%), tibialis anterior EMG (+31%) and voluntary activation (+3%) increased after glucocorticoid treatment (p<0.05). The increase in voluntary activation was associated with the gain in MVC torque (r = 0.56; p = 0.032). The level of SICI and the duration of the EMG silent period that followed the test TMS decreased (-18.6% and -13.5%, respectively) during the 50% MVC after treatment (p<0.05) while no significant change was observed for ICF. Neither SICI nor ICF changed after treatment when assessed at rest.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Short-term dexamethasone treatment induced specific decrease in the excitability of intracortical inhibitory circuits that likely contributed to the increase in the voluntary activation and associated MVC torque.
